picks.reasoning: Chovy against Knight is the whole series and I won't pretend it's a gimme: Knight has been eating mids alive, and Viper can drag any game into a scramble. But GEN has the stronger player in more roles, with Ruler and Canyon driving early tempo, and Chovy and Ruler don't wilt on leftover picks in Fearless. The LCK-over-LPL gap is real here too, so BLG steals a game with Knight's chaos, and GEN closes the other three.

usedLessons.text: Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but a star's lane edge only counts if it turns into a lead that carries past the early game, so I should stop assuming three lane advantages beat one elite player like Creme who can pull games into a scramble. Next time I'll weigh whether the stronger players can actually close games when a rival star neutralizes the map. I won't let BLG's depth or the crowd's hype carry a confident 2-0. (from Swiss BLG vs TES; picked BLG 2-0, actual TES 2-1)

Top lesson: One win doesn't prove my Chovy-over-Rookie call, because the debate showed GEN took early tempo and the map, not that Chovy won lane. Next time I'll back the side whose players are stronger across several roles, especially jungle and bot, since that's what builds early tempo, and not lean on a single marquee lane. (from Swiss GEN vs IG; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but I have to judge it by who is actually winning their matchup now, and Knight beating Zeka in mid showed that a past final win and a "best pair" label don't settle a lane. When I name one matchup as my only way to be wrong, I should treat it as the main thing to check before I pick, not a disclaimer I attach to a pick I've already made. (from Swiss HLE vs BLG; picked HLE 2-1, actual BLG 2-0)

Top lesson: When the player gap is this lopsided, stop penciling in a "stolen game" for the underdog. Fearless only drains comfort picks from players who lack the skill to win on the leftovers, and Chovy and Ruler aren't those players. Next time, back the sweep and let the stronger players finish the job. (from Quarterfinals GEN vs LYON; picked GEN 3-1, actual GEN 3-0)

BLG's early blood is real, with Knight's Orianna priority and Jarvan or Lee Sin skirmishes giving them a path to one fast game, but it hasn't reliably become gold or map control, and the LCK-over-LPL gap is showing up in who converts. I take GEN to close it out, but BLG's early-fight game steals one.

usedLessons.text: Jungle lesson: If my read says one side owns the first 15 minutes (Herald, first dragon, first tower), I shouldn't hedge with a "stolen game" built on one Swiss comeback anecdote, because that contradicts my own thesis. Before giving the underdog a game, I need to name how they'd win the early map, such as a fearless draft that leaves them tempo picks. If they can't, I call the sweep. (from Quarterfinals GEN vs LYON; picked GEN 3-1, actual GEN 3-0)

Jungle lesson: GEN won because Canyon owned the first 15 minutes (the Herald and dragon tempo I flagged), so when a team with a proven jungle edge faces an early-aggro opponent, I should trust the tempo matchup and lean harder instead of hedging at 57. HLE's blood-in-the-first-five setups only matter if they convert into objectives, so next time I'll check whether they've actually turned early kills into Herald and towers against this opponent before fearing the snowball. (from Swiss GEN vs HLE; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

Jungle lesson: The early game still decides everything, so when a big region gap is flagged, I should confirm it shows up as first-15-minute tempo (jungle pathing, lane priority, first objectives) and not lean on star names or records. I can also borrow Mid's draft point: a deep draft is what hands you that early priority, so I'll check whether a team's picks set up the first tower and dragon before I raise my confidence. (from Swiss GEN vs IG; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

Jungle lesson: Tempo is decided by who turns early pressure into first dragon and Herald, not by which champions sound aggressive in draft, so I'll weigh each team's recent objective conversion and what their support enables, such as CoreJJ's setups for an early-priority jungler, above jungle pick names. A big region gap still sets my baseline, but if the underdog's early game is clearly cleaner, I'll stop assuming the favorite's lead will hold and lean toward the sweep. (from Swiss TLAW vs AL; picked AL 2-1, actual TLAW 2-0)

I'm weighing GEN's habit of converting leads against BLG's early-game numbers, and checking whether BLG's strong first blood and first dragon rates actually turn into gold leads, which they don't seem to at Worlds. picks.reasoning: It's a draft final, and GEN's book is simply deeper: Chovy can flip between Ryze, Galio and Syndra, the jungle can switch between Lee Sin, Qiyana and Jarvan, and Ruler is on comfort picks. BLG's real weapons are Knight's Orianna and the Yunara/Lulu pair. Under Fearless those get spent early, and the LCK-over-LPL gap is the tiebreaker on top of the draft read. I'm giving BLG one game because Knight is in form and an Orianna/Yunara/Lulu draft with Jarvan or Lee priority can snowball. If BLG locks that core in game 1 and GEN can't answer the jungle tempo, I'm dropping this to a coin flip. But GEN's answers don't look thin, so I expect them to close it out in four.

usedLessons.text: Mid lesson: I called the exact draft threat (Creme on Ryze/Orianna with Lee Sin priority) and still backed BLG at 66, so when a Fearless series hinges on a pick I can't confirm BLG will deny, I should shrink my confidence instead of trusting their deeper book to cover it. Pool depth only wins if it's drafted around the opponent's best comfort picks, and I should state that flip trigger as a confidence cap before the series, not as a post-match excuse. (from Swiss BLG vs TES; picked BLG 2-1, actual TES 2-1)

Mid lesson: In a Bo1, the draft decides the game, so I'll keep naming the exact picks and bans that would flip me (Ryze or Lee Sin priority, a free Caitlyn) and check whether they actually happened, rather than crediting the draft because the pick won. When the pools are close, a flagged BIG REGION GAP is a legitimate tiebreaker that sits on top of the draft read and never replaces it. (from Swiss BLG vs KC; picked BLG, actual BLG 1-0)

Mid lesson: Under Fearless Draft, a narrow pool is a liability. When the underdog's best weapons sit in one or two signature pairs, like Berserker's Lucian/Yunara with an Alistar/Lulu engage, and the favorite has deep pools with its stars on comfort picks, I should expect those weapons to be spent early and price the sweep, not a "stolen game." I'll only keep the 3-1 if the underdog shows real depth beyond its first-rotation picks. (from Quarterfinals GEN vs LYON; picked GEN 3-1, actual GEN 3-0)

Mid lesson: When my draft read shows the favorite's pool covering the underdog's one winning script (here, Lee Sin/Jarvan answering Naafiri and Chovy's triangle surviving the lockouts), I shouldn't hand the underdog a "steal game" just because that script is possible. Under Fearless, a deeper pool means the underdog's first-rotation window shrinks as the series goes on, so I should price that edge as a sweep and keep the hedge for when the favorite's answers are actually thin. (from Semifinals GEN vs IG; picked GEN 3-1, actual GEN 3-0)

Chovy's side has finished leads and clawed back from deep holes without ever throwing one, while BLG, Knight and all, have thrown three leads and their 82% first-blood rate only shows they start fast, not that they close. BLG are no pushovers: First Stand champions, MSI finalists, and LCK is just 5-7 against the LPL this year, so I'm giving them a game or two rather than a sweep, and I stay short of 75 because a Bo5 still has variance.

usedLessons.text: ADC lesson: A single flashy number like IG's 90% first-blood rate is only tempo, not a won game, until I check whether it converted into wins against strong opponents and survived the head-to-head, and GEN's 8.4k swing in the Swiss meeting already said it didn't. When record, head-to-head and game-length tendencies all point the same way, I should price the sweep instead of reflexively shaving a game off for one stat. (from Semifinals GEN vs IG; picked GEN 3-1, actual GEN 3-0)

ADC lesson: When the head-to-head cuts both ways, I should add up every series and game between the two teams (BLG's 3-1 knockout win and HLE's 3-2 final) instead of letting one headline result tip the pick. If the combined record is close to even, my confidence should sit near 50 and not shade toward a story, even when the region flag leans that way. (from Swiss HLE vs BLG; picked HLE 2-1, actual BLG 2-0)

ADC lesson: The head-to-head record (now 7-1) and the comeback numbers lined up with the result, so when those cleaner stats agree, I can lean harder, and a flashy stat like HLE's 71% first blood should get less weight when GEN's record from behind and HLE's zero comeback wins contradict what it implies. I'll keep weighing the whole set of numbers, such as records, head-to-heads and game-length tendencies, instead of letting one headline stat decide, and I'll stay cautious in a best of 1, where one game gives us little data. (from Swiss GEN vs HLE; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

ADC lesson: When a flagged big region gap and a direct head-to-head (HLE's 3-0 at MSI) point the same way, I should lean on them and set confidence by that agreement, not by hype about individual players or a "calm room." One clean 2-0 doesn't show 68 was too low, because a Bo3 stays high-variance and my confidence should still come from the numbers, not from the sweep. usedLessons.text: Support lesson: I was right that GEN's composure counted, but I'm not going to claim the win was proof of chemistry when Canyon's early control and Chovy's comfortable draft explain much of it. Next time I'll look for concrete signs of how a team's mood shows up, such as clean early rotations, calls made under pressure and whether leads get closed out, and I'll use them to judge how far the calm room matters instead of just assuming it. (from Swiss GEN vs HLE; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

Support lesson: A team's chemistry only matters if it changes the scoreboard, and LYON's calm kept them starting from behind while GEN's composure and coaching-led drafting never cracked, so I should read both rooms before giving the underdog's good vibes a stolen game. When the favorite's room is just as steady and its prep is sharper (GEN drafting around LYON's burned picks), I should trust that the better-prepared team keeps control and not assume a warm underdog will find a comeback. (from Quarterfinals GEN vs LYON; picked GEN 3-1, actual GEN 3-0)

Support lesson: When both rooms look calm, I should trust the one whose calm shows up in concrete habits, like clean rotations and leads closed out, and not hedge a game to the other side's fast starts. A settled core that has already beaten that opponent is the stronger chemistry signal, so I'll back it without needing region talk to justify the pick. (from Semifinals GEN vs IG; picked GEN 3-1, actual GEN 3-0)

Support lesson: Chemistry still decides series, but I should read both rooms in the current moment, not lean on one past episode like DK's calm against T1, and ask which team's morale is rising and which is just holding steady. When one side looks loose and together after a big win (as BLG did after beating HLE), I should treat that momentum as stronger evidence than the other side's steadiness, and not call a five-game war on the strength of one comeback story.
